title: Diwali: The Festival of Lights
bigQuestion: Why do so many families light lamps at Diwali?

story.title: A Flower by the Door
story.kicker: A girl draws a rangoli flower by the front door and sets a tiny lamp in the middle.
paragraphs: It is a cool autumn evening. Priya kneels by her front door. She has little bowls of colored powder. Red, yellow, green and blue.
She pinches some red powder. She lets it fall in a curvy line. Line by line, a big flower grows. Her grandma helps with the petals.
Then Priya holds a tiny clay lamp. Her dad lights it for her. She sets it in the middle of the flower. The little flame dances.
"Now the house is ready," says Grandma. "Happy Diwali!" Inside, the whole family is getting ready for the festival of lights.
story.think: Priya made something beautiful to welcome people. How does your family get ready for a special day?

lessons.title: What Is Diwali?
lessons.mainIdea: Diwali is a festival of lights in the autumn.
reading: *Diwali* is a festival of lights. It comes in the autumn, in October or November. In many places it lasts five days.
Families clean their homes. They light lamps. They wear new clothes. They visit family and share sweets. It is a very happy time.

words.d: the festival of lights in the autumn
the season when leaves fall; also called fall

look.title: Five Happy Days
look.text: Look at the calendar on the fridge. Five days in a row have little stars. A boy points to the middle day. "That is the big night of lights," his mom says.
look.prompt: Why might a festival last more than one day?

lessons.title: Little Clay Lamps
lessons.mainIdea: Families light little clay lamps called diyas.
reading: A *diya* is a small clay lamp. It holds oil and a cotton wick. Families light many diyas at Diwali.
They set diyas by doors and windows. They set them on steps. The whole house glows in the dark night.

words.d: a small clay lamp with oil and a wick

look.title: Rows of Lights
look.text: Look at the steps of the house. A diya sits on each step. Tiny flames flicker in a row. The windows glow gold. The night is dark, but the house is bright.
look.prompt: How does the house look different with all the lamps?

check.why: A diya holds oil and a cotton wick.

check.q: Where do families set diyas?
check.why: Families set diyas by doors, windows and steps.

lessons.title: Different Stories, One Festival
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu families remember different stories at Diwali.
reading: Many Hindus remember Rama and Sita coming home. People lit lamps to welcome them. Other Hindus honor Lakshmi. She is the goddess of good fortune.
In South India, many remember a story of Krishna. The stories are different. The lights are the same.

words.d: the goddess of good fortune, honored by many Hindus at Diwali

look.title: Two Friends, Two Stories
look.text: Look at two friends at school. Asha says, "At Diwali, we remember Rama coming home." Dev says, "At Diwali, my family honors Lakshmi." They both smile. They both light lamps.
look.prompt: Can two families keep the same festival with different stories? How?

lessons.title: Lakshmi Puja
lessons.mainIdea: Many families honor Lakshmi with a puja on Diwali night.
reading: A *puja* is a time of worship. On Diwali night, many families do a Lakshmi puja. They gather at the home shrine.
They offer flowers, lamps and sweets. They sing. Many say Lakshmi is welcome in a clean, bright home.

words.d: a time of worship, with offerings like flowers and lamps

look.title: Lakshmi on the Lotus
look.text: The old texts describe Lakshmi rising from the ocean, seated on a lotus flower and holding lotus flowers.
look.cite: Retold from the Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chapter 9

check.why: A puja is a time of worship with offerings.

lessons.title: Diwali for Sikhs and Jains
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhs and Jains keep Diwali too, for their own reasons.
reading: Hindus are not the only people who keep Diwali. Sikhs light lamps too. They remember Guru Hargobind being set free.
Jains keep Diwali too. They remember their great teacher Mahavira. Each faith has its own reason. Each lights lamps.

words.d: a person who follows the Sikh faith
a person who follows the Jain faith

lessons.title: Rangoli Patterns
lessons.mainIdea: Families make rangoli patterns to welcome guests.
reading: *Rangoli* is a pattern made on the floor. People use colored powder, rice or flower petals.
Families make rangoli by the door. It says, "Welcome!" Many rangoli have flowers, dots, lines and circles.

words.d: a colorful pattern made on the floor with powder, rice or petals

look.text: Look at the rangoli. It starts with dots in rows. Next come lines that join the dots. Then petals fill the spaces. Last, a diya goes in the middle.

lessons.title: Diwali in Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu families in Illinois celebrate Diwali too.
reading: Many Hindu families live in Illinois. They celebrate Diwali at home. Many go to a temple too.
The Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago is in Lemont. Families visit temples like it at Diwali. Some schools share Diwali with their classes.

words.d: a building where people gather to worship

lessons.title: Light Over Dark
lessons.mainIdea: Many families say Diwali's lights stand for good winning over bad.
reading: At Diwali, lamps shine in the dark. Many families say this is a sign. Light wins over darkness.
Many say it also means good wins over bad. Kindness wins over meanness. The lights help people remember.

words.d: something that stands for an idea
